newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn may restrict spending early in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Bonn may restrict spending early in 1997.

text.p: The German government may put sharp restrictions on its spending early in 1997, government officials said.

In a letter to cabinet members quoted in Tuesday's Bild newspaper, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said, "In view of the tight budget situation ... a rule can be foreseen for 1997 that would require all spending decisions with financial effects be subject to the availability of budget funds."
Waigel wants to approve all government outlays personally, Bild reported.

Germany, a loud advocate of strict application of the Maastricht Treaty's rules for lowering government debt and deficits ahead of European economic and monetary union (EMU), is itself struggling to meet the criteria in 1997, the year when the initial EMU participants will be decided.

A Finance Ministry spokesman confirmed that the letter was authentic, but said it was a routine year-end matter. The 1997 budget will take effect on January 1 without a spending freeze, the spokesman said.

Bild quoted Juergen Koppelin, budget expert for the Free Democrats, as saying, "Waigel's decree means nothing other than a new spending freeze in the immediate future. I firmly believe it will happen in January."
Shortfalls in tax revenues caused by the economic slowdown forced Waigel to institute spending freezes in March 1996 and October 1995.
Koppelin said persistent high unemployment posed new risks for the federal budget. "Only iron-clad austerity will allow us to fulfil the Maastricht criteria for monetary union," he said.
